p.seg: <Tú Guó>
"Tú Guó"
Wú Qǐ wore scholar's robes and used military strategy to meet with Wèi Wénhóu.
Wénhóu said:
"I do not enjoy military matters."
Qǐ said:
"Your servant uses what is visible to predict what is hidden,
and uses the past to observe the future.
Why does my lord say something that contradicts his heart?
Now, you, my lord, have leather separated and cut during the four seasons,
covered with red lacquer,
Painted with cinnabar and azure,
adorned with rhinoceros horn and ivory.
In winter, wearing them does not provide warmth,
in summer, wearing them does not provide coolness.
Making long *jǐ* spears that are twenty-four *zhàng* long,
short *jǐ* spears that are twelve *zhàng* long.
Leather chariots with covered doors,
curtains on the wheels enclosing the hubs,
looking at them with the eyes, they are not beautiful,
riding them in the fields, they are not light.
I do not understand what our lord uses these for.
If they are meant to prepare for advancing in battle and retreating to defend,
but you do not seek those who can use them,
it is like a brooding hen attacking a wildcat,
or a nursing dog confronting a tiger.
Although they have a fighting spirit,
they will surely die because of it.
In the past, the ruler of the Chéngsāng Shì [承桑氏],
cultivated virtue and abandoned military affairs,
and thereby destroyed his state.
The ruler of the Yǒuhù Shì [有扈氏],
relied on his large army and loved bravery,
and thereby lost his state.
A wise ruler takes these as a lesson,
and will certainly cultivate civil virtue internally,
and govern military preparations externally.
Therefore, facing the enemy and not advancing
is not in accordance with righteousness;
stiff corpses, and mourning them
is not in accordance with benevolence."
Thereupon, Wénhóu [文侯] himself spread out the mat,
his wife held the wine cup,
and offered a libation to Wú Qǐ [吳起] in the temple,
and appointed him as Great General.
to guard the Xī Hé region.
He engaged the various lords in seventy-six major battles,
winning sixty-four outright,
with the rest ending in a draw.
He expanded the borders on all sides,
adding a thousand *lǐ* of territory,
all thanks to the achievements of Wú Qǐ.
Wú Zǐ said:
"Those who planned for the state in ancient times
surely first taught the common people and befriended all the people.
There are four kinds of disharmony:
if there is disharmony within the state,
one cannot send out troops;
if there is disharmony within the army,
one cannot deploy formations;
if there is disharmony within the formations,
one cannot advance to battle;
if there is disharmony within the battle,
one cannot achieve victory.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler,
when about to employ his people,
First achieve harmony and then undertake great affairs.
Not daring to trust in their private plans,
they must report to the ancestral temple,
inquire of the primal tortoise shell,
consult with the timing of Heaven,
only then, if it is auspicious, do they act.
When the people know that the ruler cherishes their lives
and pities their deaths,
if it reaches this point,
and he faces hardship with them,
then the soldiers will regard dying for him as an honor
and retreating to live as a disgrace."
Wú Zǐ 吳子 said:
"The Dao 道 is that by which one returns to the root and restores the beginning.
Righteousness (Yì 義) is that by which one conducts affairs and establishes merit.
Planning (Móu 謀) is that by which one avoids harm and attains benefit.
The essential (Yào 要) is that by which one protects one's enterprise and maintains accomplishment.
If actions do not accord with the Dao,
and undertakings do not accord with Righteousness,
yet one occupies a high position and lives in luxury,
misfortune will certainly befall them.
Therefore, the Sage pacifies them with the Dao,
orders them with Righteousness,
Move them with propriety,
comfort them with benevolence.
These four virtues,
if cultivated, will lead to prosperity;
if abandoned, will lead to decline.
Therefore, Chéng Tāng's 成湯 campaign against Jié 桀 brought joy to the people of the Xià 夏 dynasty,
and Zhōu Wǔ's 周武 attack on Zhòu 紂 was not criticized by the people of Yīn 殷.
Their actions accorded with the will of Heaven and the people,
therefore they were able to do so."
Wú Zǐ 吳子 said:
"In governing a state and managing an army,
one must teach them with propriety,
encourage them with righteousness,
and instill in them a sense of shame.
If people have a sense of shame,
they will be sufficient to fight in great affairs,
and sufficient to defend in small affairs.
However, winning a battle is easy,
but maintaining victory is difficult.
Therefore, it is said:
In a world of warring states,
five victories bring disaster,
four victories bring exhaustion,
three victories bring hegemony,
two victories bring kingship,
and one victory brings emperorship.
Therefore, those who gain the world through numerous victories are rare,
and many perished."
Wú Zǐ said:
"Generally, there are five reasons why wars arise:
first, contending for fame;
second, contending for profit;
third, accumulating resentment;
fourth, internal disorder;
fifth, because of famine.
There are also five types of armies:
first, a righteous army;
second, a powerful army;
third, an inflexible army;
fourth, a tyrannical army;
fifth, a rebellious army.
Suppressing tyranny and rescuing the chaotic is called righteousness;
relying on numbers to attack is called powerful;
raising troops because of anger is called inflexible;
abandoning propriety and being greedy for profit is called tyrannical;
when the state is in disorder, the people are exhausted, and actions are taken to mobilize the masses, this is called rebellious.
The methods for dealing with these five types
each have their own way.
For righteousness, one must use propriety to subdue;
for power, one must use humility to subdue;
for inflexibility, one must use rhetoric to subdue;
for tyranny, one must use deception to subdue;
for rebellion, one must use authority to subdue."
Wǔ hóu asked,
"I wish to hear the way to govern the army, assess people, and secure the state."
Qǐ replied,
"The enlightened kings of old
invariably paid careful attention to the etiquette between ruler and subject,
cultivated proper decorum between superiors and inferiors,
pacified and gathered officials and people,
educated them in accordance with customs,
and selected and recruited worthy talents
to prepare for unforeseen circumstances.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí recruited 50,000 soldiers
and thereby became the hegemon among the feudal lords.
Duke Wén of Jìn summoned 40,000 to serve as the vanguard
and thereby achieved his ambitions.
Duke Mù of Qín established a "Trap Formation" of 30,000
and thereby subdued neighboring enemies.
Therefore, the ruler of a strong state
must assess his people.
Those among the people who possess courage and strength
should be gathered into one unit.
Those who are happy to advance in battle and exert effort, to demonstrate their loyalty and bravery,
should be gathered into one unit.
Those who are capable of leaping high and reaching far, with light feet and skilled running,
should be gathered into one unit.
Those ministers of the king who have lost their positions but wish to display merit to their superiors,
should be gathered into one unit.
Those who have abandoned cities and deserted their posts, wishing to erase their shame,
should be gathered into one unit.
These five elements
are what make an army well-trained and sharp.
Having these three thousand men,
they can break through encirclements from within,
and they can slaughter a city from without."
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"I wish to hear the principles of formations that are sure to be fixed, defense that is sure to be secure, and battles that are sure to be won."
Qǐ replied,
"That can be seen immediately,
why just hear about it!
If you can make the worthy reside above,
and the unworthy be placed below,
then the formation is already fixed.
If the people are secure in their fields and houses,
and are close to their officials,
then the defense is already secure.
If the common people all regard our ruler as their own and not the neighboring countries',
then the battle is already won."
Wǔ Hóu once deliberated on a matter and his decision was correct,
none of the assembled officials could match it,
and he dismissed the court with a joyful expression.
Qǐ stepped forward and said,
"In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ once deliberated on a matter and his decision was correct,
none of the assembled officials could match it,
and he withdrew from court with a worried expression.
Shēn Gōng asked,
"Your Majesty has a worried expression,
why is that?"
He said:
"I have heard that
the world never lacks sages,
the state never lacks men of worth.
He who obtains a teacher becomes a king,
he who obtains a friend becomes a hegemon.
Now I, being untalented,
and none of my ministers able to reach me,
the state of Chǔ (楚) is in danger."
This is what King Zhuāng of Chǔ (楚莊王) was worried about,
and Your Majesty delights in it,
I, your servant, am secretly afraid."
Thereupon, Marquis Wǔ (武侯) showed a ashamed expression.
<Assessing the Enemy>
*Assessing the Enemy*
Marquis Wǔ (武侯) said to Wú Qǐ (吳起):
"Now Qín (秦) threatens us from the west,
Chǔ (楚) girds us from the south,
Zhào (趙) assaults us from the north,
Qí (齊) overlooks us from the east,
Yān (燕) cuts off our rear,
Hán (韓) occupies our front.
The six states surround and guard us on all sides,
the situation is very inconvenient,
I worry about this, what should be done?"
Qǐ (起) responded, saying:
"The way to secure a state and pacify the country
is to regard being prepared as the most valuable thing.
Now that you, my lord, are already prepared,
disaster will be far away.
Allow me to discuss the customs of the Six States:
The formations of Qí (齊) are heavy but not firm,
the formations of Qín (秦) are scattered and fight each other,
the formations of Chǔ (楚) are orderly but do not last long,
the formations of Yān (燕) are defensive and do not advance,
the formations of the Three Jìn (三晉) are well-ordered but not effective."
"The people of Qí (齊) are of a rigid nature,
their country is wealthy,
the ruler and his ministers are arrogant, extravagant, and neglectful of the common people.
Their governance is lenient, but rewards are not distributed evenly.
Within a single formation, there are two minds,
the front is heavily weighted, and the rear is lightly weighted,
therefore, it is heavy but not firm.
The way to attack this is
to divide it into three sections,
hunt down its left and right flanks,
coerce it into submission,
and its formation can be broken.
The people of Qín (秦) are of a strong nature,
their land is treacherous,
their government is strict,
Their rewards and punishments are credible,
their people do not yield,
all have a fighting spirit,
therefore they scatter and fight on their own.
The way to attack them
is to first show them profit and lure them away.
The soldiers, greedy for gain, will desert their general.
Take advantage of their discord to hunt down the scattered elements,
set up ambushes, seize opportunities,
and their general can be captured.
The state of Chǔ's 楚 nature is weak,
its territory is vast,
its government is turbulent,
its people are weary,
therefore, though they form ranks, they do not last long.
The way to attack them
is to raid and disrupt their encampments
and first seize their morale.
Advance lightly and retreat quickly,
wear them down and exhaust them,
do not engage them in battle,
and their army can be defeated.
The state of Yān's 燕 nature is sincere,
its people are cautious,
they value courage and righteousness,
and have few deceptive strategies,
therefore they defend and do not flee.
The way to attack them
If you confront and press them,
encroach and distance yourself,
dash ahead and then fall back,
then the ruler will be suspicious and those below will be fearful.
Carefully guarding the roads our chariots and cavalry must take,
their general can be captured.
The Three Jìn (Sān Jìn) states
are located in the Central Plain (Zhōngguó).
Their nature is moderate,
their governance is fair,
their people are weary of war,
but accustomed to arms.
They belittle their generals,
and provide meager salaries.
The soldiers have no will to die,
therefore, although well-governed, they are ineffective.
The way to attack them
is to block their formations and overwhelm them,
if they come in numbers, then resist them;
if they withdraw, then pursue them,
in order to exhaust their army.
This is their weakness.
"However, within an army,
there must be brave soldiers (hǔ bēn zhī shì);
with strength enough to lift a tripod,
and feet swift as warhorses.
To seize flags and decapitate generals,
There must be capable men.
Those of this kind,
select and distinguish them,
love and value them.
This is called military command.
Those who are skilled in the use of the five weapons, who are strong and swift, and whose ambition is to devour the enemy,
must have their ranks increased,
so that they can achieve victory.
Treat their parents, wives, and children well,
encourage rewards and fear punishments.
These are the soldiers who will stand firm in formation,
and can be relied upon for a long time.
If you can carefully assess this,
you can defeat twice your number."
Wǔ Hóu said:
"Good."
Wú Zǐ said:
"Generally, in assessing the enemy, there are eight cases where one can engage in battle without divination:
First, in rapid wind and great cold,
they rise early and move camp frequently,
clearing wood and crossing water,
not fearing hardship;
Second, in the height of summer heat,
they rise late without rest,
march driven by hunger and thirst,
intent on capturing distant places;
Third, their army has been bogged down for a long time,
Without provisions,
the people are resentful and angry,
ominous signs arise frequently,
the ruler is unable to stop them;
fourth, military supplies are exhausted,
firewood and fodder are scarce,
the weather is often cloudy and rainy,
there is nowhere to plunder;
fifth, the number of followers is not large,
the watery terrain is unfavorable,
people and horses are sick with disease,
neighboring regions do not come to help;
sixth, the road is long and the day is late,
the soldiers are weary and fearful,
tired and not yet fed,
they remove their armor to rest;
seventh, the general is weak and the officers are inexperienced,
the soldiers are not steadfast,
the army is frequently alarmed,
the troops have no assistance;
eighth, the battle lines are not yet set,
the camp is not yet completed,
traveling over slopes and traversing dangers,
half concealed and half exposed.
In all such cases,
attack them without hesitation.
"There are six cases where one should avoid conflict without divination:
First, extensive territory and
a wealthy and numerous populace;
second, the ruler loves his subjects and
kindness and favor are widely bestowed;
third, rewards are credible and punishments are clear;
actions are always timely;
fourth, merits are recorded and positions are assigned accordingly,
the worthy are appointed and the able are employed;
fifth, numerous instructors and disciples and
well-equipped and elite soldiers;
sixth, the assistance of neighboring states and
the support of major powers.
If all these are not as good as the enemy's,
avoid them without hesitation.
This is what is meant by advancing when it is feasible and
retreating when it is known to be difficult."
Wǔ Hóu asked:
"I wish to observe the enemy's exterior in order to understand their interior,
to examine their advance in order to know their retreat,
and thereby determine victory or defeat.
Is it possible to hear about this?"
Qǐ replied:
"When the enemy comes
carefree and without worry,
with banners and flags in disarray,
men and horses frequently looking back,
one can attack ten,
Be sure to leave them at a loss.
When the lords gather in a great assembly,
ruler and ministers are not yet in harmony,
the moats and ramparts are not yet complete,
prohibitions and commands have not yet been implemented,
the three armies are uneasy and restless,
wanting to advance but unable to,
wanting to retreat but not daring to,
use half the strength to attack double the enemy,
and a hundred battles will not be endangered."
Wǔ Hóu asked about the way to certainly defeat the enemy.
Qǐ answered,
"In employing troops, one must carefully examine the enemy's strengths and weaknesses and attack their vulnerability.
If the enemy has come from afar and is newly arrived, with their ranks not yet settled, attack them.
If they have just eaten and are not yet prepared, attack them.
If they are fleeing, attack them.
If they are fatigued, attack them.
If they have not yet secured advantageous terrain, attack them.
If they miss the opportune moment and do not follow orders, attack them.
If their flags and banners are in disarray, attack them.
If they have traversed a long road and the rear ranks have not yet rested, attack them.
If they are halfway across a river, attack them.
If they are on a dangerous path or a narrow road, attack them.
If the formations are constantly shifting, attack them.
If the general is estranged from his soldiers, attack them.
If their hearts are filled with fear, attack them.
In all such cases,
Select the sharpest troops to charge,
divide the forces to follow up,
and attack quickly without hesitation."
"Governing the Army"
*Governing the Army*
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"What is the priority in advancing troops?"
Qǐ replied,
"First, understand the four lightnesses, two heavinesses, and one trustworthiness."
(Wǔ Hóu) said,
"What do you mean?"
(Qǐ) replied,
"Make the ground feel light to the horses,
the horses feel light to the chariots,
the chariots feel light to the men,
and the men feel light to battle.
Clearly understand the terrain and weather,
then the ground will feel light to the horses.
Provide fodder at the right time,
then the horses will feel light to the chariots.
Have ample grease and maintenance,
then the chariots will feel light to the men.
Have sharp weapons and strong armor,
then the men will feel light to battle.
Have heavy rewards for advancing
and heavy punishments for retreating.
Execute it with trustworthiness.
Commands and regulations are far-reaching,
this is the ruler who achieves victory."
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"How does an army achieve victory?"
Qǐ replied,
"It achieves victory through order."
He further asked,
"Does it not depend on the size of the force?"
Qǐ replied,
"If the laws and regulations are unclear,
rewards and punishments are not credible,
the gong cannot stop them,
the drum cannot advance them,
even with a million soldiers,
what benefit is there in using them?
What is meant by 'order' is:
when at rest, there is propriety;
when in motion, there is authority;
advancing, they cannot be stopped;
retreating, they cannot be pursued;
advancing and retreating have rhythm;
left and right respond to the command;
even if broken up, they form ranks;
even if scattered, they form lines.
Share peace with them,
If you share danger with them,
their multitude can be united but not separated,
they can be employed but not exhausted.
Throw them where they are going,
nothing in the world can match them.
This is called "father and son troops."
Wú Zǐ said:
"Generally, the way of conducting an army
is never to violate the proper timing of advance and retreat,
never to miss the proper moderation in food and drink,
never to exhaust the strength of men and horses.
These three things
are the means by which to ensure obedience to the orders from above.
When the orders from above are obeyed,
then order is produced.
If advance and retreat are not measured,
food and drink are not moderate,
and horses and men are exhausted and weary without being given rest,
then obedience to the orders from above will be impossible.
Once the orders from above are abandoned,
occupying territory will lead to disorder,
and engaging in battle will lead to defeat."
Wú Zǐ said:
"Generally, the battlefield
is a place where corpses are erected.
Certain death results in life,
Fortunately there is life, then there is death.
The good commander,
is like being in a leaking boat,
or crouching beneath a burning house.
He makes the wise unable to strategize,
and the brave unable to become angry.
Thus, he can withstand the enemy.
Therefore, it is said:
"The greatest harm in employing troops
is hesitation;
the disaster of the army
arises from suspicion and doubt."
Wú Zǐ said:
"People fail when they attempt what they are incapable of,
and are defeated when they attempt what is not advantageous.
Therefore, in the art of war,
instruction and training come first.
One person learns to fight,
and then teaches ten people.
Ten people learn to fight,
and then teach one hundred people.
One hundred people learn to fight,
and then teach one thousand people.
One thousand people learn to fight,
and then teach ten thousand people.
Ten thousand people learn to fight,
and then teach the entire army.
To await the distant by being near,
to await the weary by being at ease,
to await the hungry by being full.
To make the round square,
to make the sitting rise,
to make the moving stop,
to make the left go right,
to make the front go back,
to divide and then unite,
to bind and then release.
Every change should be practiced,
then give him troops.
This is called "commanding affairs."
Wú Zǐ said:
"In the order for teaching battle,
the short should wield spears and halberds,
the tall should wield bows and crossbows,
the strong should hold banners,
the brave should hold metal drums,
the weak should provide provisions and care,
the wise should be strategists.
Villages and neighborhoods should be adjacent to each other,
groups of ten and five should protect each other.
At the first drum, arrange the troops,
at the second drum, practice formations,
at the third drum, hasten to eat,
at the fourth drum, strictly distinguish,
At the fifth watch of the night, set out.
When you hear the sound of the drums uniting
then raise the banners."
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"Are there principles
for the advance and retreat of the three armies?"
Qǐ replied,
"Do not be stationed facing the 'Heavenly Hearth' (tiānzào),
do not be stationed facing the 'Dragon's Head' (lóngtóu).
The 'Heavenly Hearth'
is the mouth of a large valley.
The 'Dragon's Head'
is the summit of a great mountain.
There must be a Green Dragon (qīnglóng) on the left,
a White Tiger (báihǔ) on the right,
a Vermillion Bird (zhūquè) in the front,
a Black Tortoise (xuánwǔ) in the rear,
Zhāoyáo above,
Cóngshì below.
When about to battle,
carefully observe from where the wind comes.
If the wind is favorable, raise a shout and follow it;
if the wind is adverse, solidify your formation and await it."
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"Are there methods
for raising soldiers and horses?"
Qǐ responded, saying:
"Indeed, horses must be comfortable in their places,
suitable for their water and grass,
and moderated in their hunger and fullness.
In winter, they should be kept warm,
in summer, in cool shelters.
Their manes should be carefully trimmed,
and their hooves meticulously cared for.
Their ears and eyes should be shielded
so as not to be startled.
They should be trained to gallop and chase,
and familiarized with starting and stopping.
When man and horse are mutually fond,
then can they be used.
The equipment for chariots and cavalry,
the saddle, bridle, bit, and reins,
must be kept complete and sturdy.
Usually, a horse is not injured in the end,
but is injured in the beginning;
not injured by hunger,
but is injured by being overfed.
When the day is late and the road is long,
one must frequently dismount.
It is better to tire the man,
than to tire the horse.
Always leave something in reserve,
in preparation for the enemy to overcome us.
He who understands these things,
héng xíng tiān xià." (to) roam freely under Heaven."
"Lùn Jiàng" (On Generals)
*Lùn Jiàng* (On Generals)
Wú Zǐ said:
"Now, one who combines civil and military skills is
the general of an army.
One who combines firmness and gentleness
is skilled in military affairs.
Generally, when people discuss generals,
they often focus on courage.
But courage in a general
is only one aspect.
For a brave person will surely engage lightly,
and if he engages lightly without knowing the advantage,
that will not do.
Thus, what a general should be cautious of are five things:
The first is *lǐ* (order),
the second is *bèi* (preparedness),
the third is *guǒ* (decisiveness),
the fourth is *jiè* (vigilance),
the fifth is *yuē* (simplicity).
*Lǐ* (Order) means
governing a large number as you would a small number.
*Bèi* (Preparedness) means
going out the door as if you were facing the enemy.
*Guǒ* (Decisiveness) means
not being attached to life when facing the enemy.
Jiè zhě,
suī kè rú shǐ zhàn.
Yuē zhě,
fǎlìng shěng ér bù fán.
Shòu mìng ér bù cí,
dí pò ér hòu yán fǎn,
jiàng zhī lǐ yě.
Gù shī chū zhī rì,
yǒu sǐ zhī róng,
wú shēng zhī rǔ."
Master Wú said:
"Generally, in warfare, there are four crucial elements:
first, the morale,
second, the terrain,
third, the circumstances,
fourth, the strength.
The masses of the three armies,
a million soldiers,
the arrangement of light and heavy forces,
rests on one person,
this is called the morale.
Narrow roads and dangerous paths,
famous mountains and great passes,
where ten men can hold,
and a thousand cannot pass,
this is called the terrain.
Being good at using spies,
To use light troops to move back and forth,
to scatter their forces,
to make their ruler and ministers resent each other,
and superiors and inferiors blame each other—
this is called *shì jī* (事機, the opportune moment).
Strong carriages that are well-managed,
boats with effective oars and rudders,
soldiers trained in battle formations,
horses accustomed to galloping and chasing—
this is called *lì jī* (力機, the means of strength).
Knowing these four things
makes one qualified to be a general.
Moreover, one's prestige (*wēi*), virtue (*dé*), benevolence (*rén*), and courage (*yǒng*)
must be sufficient to lead subordinates and pacify the masses,
frighten the enemy and resolve doubts.
When orders are given, subordinates do not violate them;
wherever one is, the enemy dares not oppose.
Obtaining such a general strengthens a state,
losing such a general destroys a state.
This is called a good general."
*Wú Zǐ* (吳子) said:
"The drums (*pí gǔ*) and metal bells (*jīn duó*)
are used to awe the ears.
The banners (*jīng qí*) and pennants (*huī zhì*)
are used to awe the eyes.
Prohibitions, orders, and punishments
are used to awe the mind.
The ear's authority lies in sound;
it must not be unclear.
The eye's authority lies in color;
it must not be lacking in discernment.
The heart's authority lies in punishment;
it must not be lacking in severity.
If these three are not established,
even if one possesses the state,
it will surely be defeated by the enemy.
Therefore, it is said:
"Wherever the general waves his banner,
all follow and shift;
wherever the general points,
all advance to their death."
Wú Zǐ said:
"In general, the key to battle
is to first assess their general and observe his abilities.
Adapt to the terrain and employ stratagem;
then you can achieve success without labor.
If their general is foolish and trusts others,
he can be deceived and lured;
if he is greedy and disregards reputation,
he can be bought and bribed;
if he is fickle and lacks planning,
he can be exhausted and besieged.
If those above are rich and arrogant,
and those below are poor and resentful,
They can be separated and alienated.
If advancing and retreating is filled with doubt,
their troops will have no support,
and they can be shocked and routed.
If the soldiers despise their general and have thoughts of returning home,
and the fortified passes are easily opened while the dangerous routes are exposed,
they can be ambushed and captured.
If the path to advance is easy,
and the path to retreat is difficult,
they can be lured forward.
If the path to advance is dangerous,
and the path to retreat is easy,
they can be pressed and attacked.
If the army is stationed in a low, damp place,
where water has no outlet,
and continuous rain frequently falls,
they can be flooded and submerged.
If the army is stationed in a desolate swamp,
where the grass and shrubs are overgrown and filthy,
and violent winds frequently blow,
they can be burned and destroyed.
If they stay for a long time without moving,
and the generals and soldiers become lax and negligent,
and their army is unprepared,
they can be secretly ambushed."
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"When two armies face each other,
"I don't know what kind of general he will be.
I want to assess him.
What methods should I use?"
Qǐ responded,
"Order a lowly but brave man
to lead a light and swift force to test him.
Focus on observing the north,
do not focus on gaining advantage.
Observe the enemy's approach.
If they rise and sit in unison,
their administration is orderly,
their pursuit of the defeated appears intentionally slow,
and when they see advantage, they pretend not to notice,
such a general
is called a wise general;
do not engage him in battle.
If their troops are clamorous,
their flags and banners are in disarray,
their soldiers advance and halt on their own,
their troops are sometimes aligned vertically and sometimes horizontally,
their pursuit of the defeated fears being too slow,
and when they see advantage, they fear not obtaining it,
this is a foolish general,
even if he has a large army, he can be defeated."
《Yìngbiàn》
*Yìngbiàn*
Wǔ Hóu asked,
If the chariots are sturdy and the horses are good,
the generals are brave and the soldiers are strong,
but when the troops encounter the enemy,
they become disorganized and lose their formation,
what should be done?"
Qǐ replied,
"Generally, the methods of warfare
are to use banners, flags, and pennants as signals during the day,
and gongs, drums, and reed pipes as signals at night.
Wave the banner to the left, and they go left;
wave it to the right, and they go right.
Beat the drum, and they advance;
strike the gong, and they stop.
Two blasts and they move,
a second blast and they gather;
those who do not follow orders shall be executed.
If the entire army is in awe of authority,
and the soldiers are willing to give their lives,
then in battle there will be no powerful enemy,
and in attack there will be no impregnable formation."
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"If the enemy is numerous and our forces are few,
what should be done?"
Qǐ replied,
"Avoid them in open terrain,
intercept them in narrow passes.
Thus it is said:
To use one to strike ten,
nothing is better than a narrow pass;
to use ten to strike a hundred,
nothing is better than a dangerous place;
to use a thousand to strike ten thousand,
nothing is better than an obstacle.
Now, if a young soldier suddenly arises
and strikes metal and beats a drum in a narrow pass,
even if there is a large crowd,
none will not be startled.
Thus it is said:
"He who employs a large force strives for ease;
he who employs a small force strives for narrowness."
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"There is an army that is very large,
both martial and brave;
backing against great dangers and obstacles,
with mountains on the right and water on the left;
deep trenches and high ramparts,
defended with strong crossbows;
retreating like the shifting of mountains,
advancing like wind and rain,
and with much food.
It is difficult to hold against them for a long time."
He replied,
"What a great question!
This is not the strength of chariots and cavalry,
but the strategy of a sage.
To be able to equip a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry,
combining them with infantry,
dividing them into five armies,
each army occupying one avenue.
With five armies and five avenues,
the enemy will surely be confused,
and not know where to attack.
If the enemy firmly defends to strengthen their forces,
swiftly send spies to observe their thoughts.
If they heed my words,
they will disperse and leave.
If they do not heed my words,
execute the envoy and burn the letter,
and divide into five battles.
If you win a battle, do not pursue;
if you lose, retreat quickly.
If you feign defeat in this way,
advance stealthily and fight quickly,
block their front,
and cut off their rear.
Two armies advance with concealed flags,
sometimes to the left, sometimes to the right,
and attack their positions.
When all five armies arrive together,
there will surely be strength.
"This is the way to strike the strong."
Wǔ Hóu 武侯 asked:
"If the enemy is close and pressing upon me,
and there is no way to retreat,
and my troops are very afraid,
what should be done?"
Qǐ ǐ replied:
"For this tactic,
if my troops are many and theirs are few,
divide and attack them.
If they are many and my troops are few,
follow them in a square formation.
Follow them without rest,
and even if they are many, they can be subdued."
Wǔ Hóu 武侯 asked:
"If we encounter the enemy in a ravine,
with many dangerous obstacles nearby,
and they are many while my troops are few,
what should be done?"
Qǐ ǐ replied:
"In all hills, forests, valleys, deep mountains, and great swamps,
move quickly and leave promptly,
do not linger.
If in high mountains and deep valleys,
you suddenly encounter them,
be sure to first raise a clamor and attack them.
Advance with bows and crossbows,
shooting and capturing at the same time.
Scrutinize their government;
if it is in disarray, attack them without hesitation."
Wǔ Hóu 武侯 asked:
"With high mountains on the left and right,
and the land being very narrow and constricted,
if we suddenly encounter the enemy,
we dare not attack them,
and we cannot retreat;
what should be done?"
Qǐ 起 replied:
"This is called a valley battle;
even a large force is useless.
Recruit skilled soldiers to be equivalent to the enemy,
with light feet and sharp weapons, to go ahead.
Divide chariots and arrayed cavalry, hidden on all four sides,
several *lǐ* 里 apart,
so that their troops are not seen.
The enemy will certainly form a solid battle formation,
daring neither to advance nor retreat.
Then, display banners and pennants,
march out of the mountains and set up camp,
and the enemy will surely be afraid.
Use chariots and cavalry to provoke them,
not allowing them to rest.
This is the method of valley warfare."
Wǔ Hóu asked:
"If I encounter the enemy in a large marsh,
with wheels overturned and axles submerged,
the water close to the carts and horses,
without boats or rafts prepared,
unable to advance or retreat,
what should be done?"
Qǐ replied:
"This is called water warfare;
carts and horses are useless;
leave them nearby.
Climb to a high place and observe in all directions;
you will surely understand the water's condition.
Know its width and narrowness,
ascertain its shallowness and depth,
then you can use surprise tactics to defeat them.
If the enemy crosses the water,
attack them when they are halfway across."
Wǔ Hóu asked:
"If it rains continuously for a long time,
horses sink and carts stop,
surrounded by enemies on all sides,
the entire army is alarmed and frightened,
what should be done?"
Qǐ replied:
"Generally, when using carts,
Where it's shady and damp, stop;
where it's sunny and dry, set off.
Value the high, disdain the low;
drive your strong chariots.
Whether advancing or stopping,
certainly follow the proper path.
If the enemy rises,
certainly pursue their tracks."
The Marquis of Wǔ asked,
"If fierce bandits suddenly come,
plunder our fields,
take our cattle and sheep,
then what should be done?"
Qǐ replied,
"When fierce bandits come,
certainly consider their strength;
defend well and do not engage.
When they are about to leave at dusk,
their baggage will certainly be heavy,
their hearts will certainly be fearful,
their return retreat will be urgent,
there will certainly be those who fall behind.
Pursue and strike them,
their army can be overturned."
Wú Zǐ said:
"Generally, the way to attack an enemy besieged city [is]:
After the cities and towns have been breached,
each should enter its palaces.
Manage their salaries and stipends,
collect their weapons and goods.
Wherever the army arrives,
do not cut down their trees, tear down their houses, take their grain, kill their livestock, or burn their stored goods,
to show the people that you have no cruel intentions.
Those who request to surrender,
accept and pacify them."
〈Lì Shì〉 ("Encouraging the Soldiers")
《Lì Shì》 ("Encouraging the Soldiers")
Wǔ Hóu asked,
"Is severe punishment and clear rewards enough to achieve victory?"
Qǐ replied,
"The details of strictness and clarity,
your servant cannot fully comprehend.
However,
these are not what one should rely on.
If issuing commands and decrees makes people happy to hear them,
if raising troops and mobilizing the masses makes people happy to fight,
and if engaging in combat and crossing blades makes people happy to die,
these three things
are what the ruler should rely on."
Wǔ Hóu said,
"How can I achieve them?"
He replied,
"If the ruler initiates an undertaking with success, then a feast is held to reward them;
if there is no success, they are encouraged."
Thereupon, Wǔ Hóu set up seats in the ancestral temple in three rows to feast the officers and gentlemen.
Those with the highest merit sat in the front row,
and their dishes and seats included heavy vessels and superior sacrificial offerings.
Those with the next highest merit sat in the middle row,
and their dishes and seats were slightly inferior.
Those with no merit sat in the back row,
and their dishes and seats had no heavy vessels.
After the feast was over,
the parents, wives, and children of those with merit were bestowed with gifts outside the temple gate,
also in accordance with the degree of merit.
For the families of those who died in service,
messengers were dispatched annually to comfort and reward their parents,
showing that they were not forgotten.
After three years of this practice,
the people of Qín raised an army
and approached the Western River.
When the Wèi soldiers heard of it,
without waiting for official orders,
tens of thousands donned armor and fought fiercely.
Wǔ Hóu summoned Wú Qǐ and said to him,
"The teaching you gave me the other day has been put into practice."
Qǐ replied,
"I have heard that people have strengths and weaknesses,
and their morale has its ups and downs.
"If Your Majesty would try to dispatch fifty thousand men who have accomplished nothing,
I, your minister, request to lead them to confront the enemy.
If they fail to win,
we will become a laughingstock among the feudal lords,
and lose authority over the realm.
Now, if a single desperate thief lies hidden in the wilderness,
and a thousand men pursue him,
none of them fail to glare fiercely and look around warily.
Why is this?
They fear his sudden attack and harm to themselves.
Thus, when one man risks his life,
it is enough to strike fear into a thousand men.
Now, I will use fifty thousand troops,
acting as a single desperate thief,
and lead them to attack;
it would certainly be difficult to resist."
Thereupon, Wǔ Hóu followed his advice,
adding five hundred chariots,
and three thousand horses,
and defeated the Qín army of five hundred thousand men.
This was the achievement of encouraging the soldiers.
On the day before the battle,
Wú Qǐ ordered the three armies, saying:
"All officers and soldiers must follow my orders.
Chariots, cavalry, and infantry,
if chariots do not function as chariots,
cavalry do not function as cavalry,
infantry do not function as infantry,
even if the army is defeated, there will be no pardon."
Therefore, on the day of battle,
his commands were not verbose, yet his authority shook the world.
